scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The `openpiv` skill is a legitimate, technically coherent Particle Image Velocimetry analysis package. All three Python scripts (runner.py, run_example.py, analyze.py) perform exactly what the manifest and instructions describe: reading local image files, running OpenPIV cross-correlation, validating/replacing vectors, saving vectors.txt / params.npz / PNG plots into a user-specified output directory, and computing vorticity, strain, and statistics with numpy. No prompt-injection, role-redefinition, concealment, or safety-bypass language appears anywhere in SKILL.md or the reference file. There are no network calls, no environment-variable or credential access (no ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, os.environ reads), no eval/exec/os.system/subprocess usage, no base64 or obfuscated payloads, and no hardcoded secrets. Argument handling uses argparse with `choices` constraints and explicit validation of window/search-area/overlap relationships; file paths come from explicit user CLI arguments and are used only with numpy/matplotlib/openpiv I/O, not shell interpolation. `sys.path.insert` in run_example.py points only at the script's own directory, which is normal for a self-contained skill. Declared `allowed-tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash` are consistent with observed behavior (reads images, writes results, runs a Python CLI). Referenced internal file references/advanced_algorithms.md contains only benign API documentation. Provenance metadata (version, author, license, tested-against) is present. Only minor hygiene issues were found: an unpinned pip install as the primary install command and a few documentation path references that do not resolve. No malicious behavior detected.

findings.title: Unpinned dependency install instruction
findings.description: The skill instructs the user to run `uv pip install openpiv` without a version pin as the primary install command (a pinned variant is offered secondarily). Unpinned installs can pull in a compromised or breaking upstream release. This is a minor supply-chain hygiene issue only; the package is the legitimate, well-known OpenPIV project and matches the skill's stated purpose.
findings.snippet:
uv pip install openpiv

# Pin it when the analysis needs to be reproducible ...
uv pip install "openpiv==0.25.4"
findings.remediation: Recommend the pinned install (`openpiv==0.25.4`) as the default instruction, since the skill documents that all snippets are verified against that version.

findings.title: References to non-existent files in instructions
findings.description: The instruction text and scripts reference several paths that do not resolve in the package listing (openpiv.py, matplotlib.py, assets/advanced_algorithms.md, templates/advanced_algorithms.md, analyze.py at top level). Most of these are false positives from module-import parsing (openpiv, matplotlib are pip packages; analyze.py exists at scripts/analyze.py, and references/advanced_algorithms.md exists). No unresolved path is fetched from a network source, so risk is documentation-quality only.
findings.snippet: Files referenced in instructions: openpiv.py, assets/advanced_algorithms.md, matplotlib.py, templates/advanced_algorithms.md, analyze.py, references/advanced_algorithms.md
findings.remediation: Use explicit relative paths (e.g., scripts/analyze.py, references/advanced_algorithms.md) in documentation to avoid ambiguity.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The opentrons-integration skill is a legitimate, documentation-heavy engineering skill for authoring Opentrons Python Protocol API v2 protocols. All five bundled Python scripts are pure Opentrons protocol templates: they import only `opentrons.protocol_api`, define metadata/requirements, and call load_labware/load_instrument/transfer/module APIs. There is no network I/O, no subprocess/eval/exec, no filesystem traversal, no environment-variable or credential access, no hardcoded secrets, and no obfuscation or encoded payloads. The SKILL.md body contains no prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, or safety-bypass language; instead it repeatedly emphasizes conservative safety practices (simulate, App analysis, operator review, dry run, emergency stop). The description accurately matches behavior and even directs users to a different skill (pylabrobot) for multi-vendor workflows, which is the opposite of capability inflation. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with the workflow of writing protocol files and running `opentrons_simulate`/`py_compile` via Bash. Referenced reference docs are internal to the package and contain only technical guidance; notably they explicitly advise against top-level network calls, downloading packages during runs, embedding credentials, and using `-D` on directories containing credentials — security-positive guidance. Residual risks are minor: pinned-but-network-dependent `uv run --with`/`uv pip install` dependency fetching, and a few unresolved referenced file paths (assets/*, templates/*, opentrons.py). Note that the skill drives physical laboratory hardware, so operational (not cyber) safety depends on the user following the documented validation ladder, which the skill adequately stresses.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This is a legitimate, well-structured technical documentation skill for GPU-accelerating Python with the NVIDIA RAPIDS/CUDA ecosystem. Despite the manifest listing 5 "python" files, no executable scripts were provided — the package consists of SKILL.md plus reference markdown files. Manual review of all supplied instruction and reference content found NO prompt injection, no instruction-override or concealment language, no jailbreak attempts, no obfuscation/encoding, no hardcoded secrets, no reads of ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, or other credential stores, no outbound network calls to attacker-controlled endpoints, and no read-then-send tool-chaining. All code examples are standard, accurate, publicly documented API usage (CuPy, cuDF, cuML, cuGraph, Warp, KvikIO, cuVS, cuCIM, cuSpatial, cuxfilter, RAFT, Numba CUDA), and the skill's own guidance advises safe practices such as CPU fallbacks and numerical-correctness validation. All referenced files resolve to internal paths within the skill package (the assets/ and templates/ "not found" entries are path-guessing artifacts of the scanner, not external fetches); no external URLs are read as instructions — the only URLs present are documentation links and NVIDIA's official package index. The static pre-scan alerts for "env var exfiltration" and "cross-file exfiltration chain" are false positives arising from KvikIO documentation that merely explains AWS credential environment variables alongside read-only S3/HTTP ingest examples; there is no data egress path anywhere in the package. Residual concerns are minor hygiene issues: an aggressively keyword-baited description that self-activates "even if not explicitly requested," unpinned dependency install commands via an extra package index, and absent allowed-tools/license/compatibility metadata. Overall risk: LOW — this skill appears safe to use with the noted metadata and dependency-pinning improvements.
llm_primary_threats: Capability inflation / over-broad activation description (keyword baiting, self-activation without explicit user request)
Unpinned dependency installation guidance via an alternate package index (minor supply-chain surface)
Missing manifest metadata (no allowed-tools, license, or compatibility declarations)

findings.title: Documentation examples reference remote data reads (S3/HTTP) and AWS credential environment variables — no exfiltration path
findings.description: Static pre-scan flagged "env var exfiltration" chains. Manual review shows the matches come solely from the KvikIO reference documentation, which explains that AWS credentials are read from AWS_DEFAULT_REGION / AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID / AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY and shows read-only examples for kvikio.RemoteFile.open_s3 / open_http. These are inbound reads to user-specified buckets/URLs, contain no attacker-controlled endpoints, and no code in the package reads credentials or transmits data anywhere. Assessed as a false positive; recorded at LOW severity for transparency only.
findings.snippet:
AWS credentials come from environment variables (`AWS_DEFAULT_REGION`, `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`) or can be passed as keyword arguments.
with kvikio.RemoteFile.open_http("https://example.com/data.bin") as f:
findings.remediation: No action strictly required. Optionally add a note that credentials should be sourced from the environment/instance role and never hardcoded or echoed into generated code, and that RemoteFile is read-only.

findings.title: Over-broad activation description encourages unsolicited skill invocation
findings.description: The skill description is extremely keyword-dense (12+ library names, ~15 workload domains) and explicitly instructs activation "even if not explicitly requested" when CPU-bound Python code is seen. This is capability/keyword inflation that increases unwanted activation, though the claimed capabilities are legitimately covered by the bundled reference material and the behavior is limited to code-rewriting advice.
findings.snippet: "Also use when you see CPU-bound Python code (loops, large arrays, ML pipelines, graph analytics, image processing) that would benefit from GPU acceleration, even if not explicitly requested."
findings.remediation: Narrow the description to explicit user intent (e.g., "use when the user asks to GPU-accelerate Python code") and remove the self-activation clause and redundant keyword lists.

findings.title: Unpinned dependency installation guidance from an alternate package index
findings.description: Reference files instruct the agent to always install packages with `uv add` without version pins, and several commands add `--extra-index-url=https://pypi.nvidia.com`. The index is NVIDIA's official RAPIDS index and the package names are legitimate, so risk is low, but unpinned installs plus an extra index broaden the supply-chain surface (dependency confusion / unexpected version drift) if the agent executes these commands.
findings.snippet:
uv add --extra-index-url=https://pypi.nvidia.com cugraph-cu12
uv add cupy-cuda12x
"Always use `uv add` (never `pip install` or `conda install`) in all install instructions..."
findings.remediation: Recommend pinned versions (e.g., cudf-cu12==26.6.*) and note that installation commands should be surfaced to the user for approval rather than executed automatically; document why the NVIDIA index is required.

findings.title: Missing allowed-tools / license / compatibility metadata
findings.description: The manifest declares only name, description, version, and author. There is no `allowed-tools` restriction, no license, and no compatibility field. Since the skill's guidance implies package installation, profiling commands (nsys, nvprof), file IO, and dashboard servers (d.show() binds a local HTTP port), absent tool restrictions mean the agent may run Bash/Python without declared bounds. Informational only — the field is optional per spec.
findings.snippet:
- license: Not specified
- compatibility: Not specified
- allowed-tools: Not specified
findings.remediation: Declare `allowed-tools` (e.g., [Read, Write, Grep, Glob]) and add license/compatibility metadata. If Bash is needed for installs, state it explicitly so the user can reason about the blast radius.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The pacsomatic skill is a legitimate bioinformatics operator toolkit for nf-core/pacsomatic. Its manifest description accurately matches the behavior of the single bundled Python helper, and the reference documents contain only ordinary usage guidance with no prompt-injection, concealment, or instruction-override language. No data exfiltration, credential access (~/.aws, ~/.ssh), environment harvesting, hardcoded secrets, base64/obfuscated payloads, or network egress of user data was found; the only outbound network activity is an optional git clone of the pipeline repository, which defaults to the official nf-core URL. The static BEHAVIOR_EVAL_SUBPROCESS hit is a false positive for eval/exec: the code uses subprocess.run() with argv lists (never shell=True) and deliberately avoids shell interpretation, including a dedicated normalize_module_load() validator that rejects shell metacharacters in --module-load and an argv-based submission path for bsub/sbatch/qsub. Residual risk is inherent to the skill's purpose: it writes an executable 0755 launch script and can submit it to a scheduler, and several caller-controlled options (--extra-args, --nxf-opts, --pipeline, --repo-url, --conda-env-file) expand what ultimately gets executed. These are MEDIUM/LOW operational concerns rather than malicious behavior. Overall the skill appears benign and reasonably defensively coded.
llm_primary_threats: Caller-controlled argument pass-through into generated/executed launch scripts (--extra-args, --nxf-opts)
Unpinned supply-chain fetch: git clone from overridable --repo-url and conda env creation from arbitrary YAML
Undeclared allowed-tools despite file-write and process-execution capabilities
Dangling references to non-existent templates/ and assets/ documentation files

findings.title: Arbitrary argument pass-through into generated launch script via --extra-args
findings.description: The helper accepts an arbitrary free-form string via --extra-args, splits it with shlex.split(), and appends the resulting tokens to the Nextflow command that is written into an executable launch script and later executed/submitted (bash/bsub/sbatch/qsub). While tokens are shlex.quote()-ed when rendered, they still become additional Nextflow CLI arguments (e.g. -c custom.config, -plugins, custom pipeline revisions), which allows a caller-controlled expansion of what the pipeline executes. Similar caller-controlled values (--nxf-opts, --pipeline, --repo-url) also flow into generated shell/exec paths. This is an intended operator convenience but represents a code-execution surface if the argument value originates from untrusted prompt content.
findings.remediation: Restrict --extra-args to an allowlist of known Nextflow flags, or require explicit user confirmation before executing a launch script that contains caller-supplied extra arguments. Document that --extra-args must never be populated from untrusted input.

findings.title: Unpinned git clone and conda environment creation from caller-specified sources
findings.description: ensure_pipeline_repo() will run `git clone` against a user-supplied --repo-url into --checkout-dir without any revision pinning or host allowlist, and create_conda_env() will invoke `mamba/conda env create` from a caller-specified YAML file. Defaults point at the legitimate nf-core repository and a bundled environment file, but overriding --repo-url allows fetching and later executing arbitrary pipeline code (main.nf and its processes) from an untrusted repository.
findings.snippet:
cmd = ["git", "clone", args.repo_url, str(target)]
...
cmd = ["mamba", "env", "create", "-n", env_name, "-f", str(env_file)]
findings.remediation: Pin the cloned revision (e.g. --pipeline-version/git checkout of a tag or commit SHA), validate --repo-url against an allowlist of trusted hosts, and surface a confirmation prompt before cloning or creating environments from non-default sources.

findings.title: No allowed-tools declared while skill performs file writes and process execution
findings.description: The YAML frontmatter omits the optional allowed-tools and compatibility fields, yet the skill writes files (samplesheet CSV, params YAML, an executable 0755 launch script) and executes external processes (nextflow, git, conda/mamba, bsub/sbatch/qsub/bash). Absence of the declaration is informational only, but it means the elevated capability profile of this skill is not explicitly disclosed in the manifest.
findings.snippet: allowed-tools: Not specified; compatibility: Not specified — script performs os.chmod(script_path, 0o755) and subprocess.run() for scheduler submission
findings.remediation: Declare allowed-tools (e.g. [Read, Write, Bash, Python]) and compatibility in the frontmatter so operators can see that the skill writes executable artifacts and spawns processes.

findings.title: Broken/missing referenced file paths in documentation index
findings.description: The static reference index lists several files under templates/ and assets/ (templates/pacsomatic_guide.md, assets/agent-playbook.md, templates/config-and-output.md, assets/pacsomatic_guide.md, assets/config-and-output.md, templates/agent-playbook.md) that do not exist in the package. Only the references/ copies are present. Dangling references are a documentation hygiene issue and could later be satisfied by attacker-planted files with the same names.
findings.snippet: Referenced File: templates/pacsomatic_guide.md (not found); assets/agent-playbook.md (not found); templates/config-and-output.md (not found)
findings.remediation: Remove or correct the non-existent templates/ and assets/ paths so only the bundled references/ files are referenced.

metadata.aisubtech_name: Safety Harms and Toxicity: Scams and Deception

findings.title: eval/exec combined with subprocess detected
findings.description: Dangerous combination of code execution and system commands in skills/pacsomatic/scripts/run_pacsomatic.py
findings.remediation: Remove eval/exec or use safer alternatives

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The paper-lookup skill is a well-engineered, defensively written academic literature retrieval package. All network activity targets well-known, legitimate scholarly APIs (NCBI/PubMed/PMC, Europe PMC, bioRxiv, arXiv, OpenAlex, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, CORE, Unpaywall) over documented endpoints; no exfiltration destinations, telemetry, or unexpected hosts were found. The four bundled Python scripts use only the standard library, contain no eval/exec/os.system/subprocess, no shell interpolation, no hardcoded secrets, and no obfuscated or encoded payloads. Notably, the skill implements several security controls rather than violating them: it explicitly instructs the agent to treat all API responses as untrusted third-party data and never follow instructions embedded in them (an anti-prompt-injection control), it redacts credential query parameters (api_key, apikey, key, email, mailto, tool) from provenance output, it caps input size at 64 MB to prevent memory exhaustion, it enforces bounded pagination (default 1,000 records / 50 calls) with per-host rate-limit delays and no parallelization against rate-limited hosts, and it requires user confirmation before exceeding those bounds. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Bash) are consistent with actual behavior (curl calls plus python3 execution of bundled scripts, all invoked via Bash); scripts write files only to caller-specified -o/--output paths. The description is keyword-rich but accurately and proportionately reflects the eleven documented databases, so it does not constitute capability inflation. Only referenced files under references/ (bundled with the package) are read; the assets/ and templates/ paths listed as \"not found\" are not actually referenced by the instructions. The single item worth flagging is the optional fallback that reads a local .env file for four named API keys — a narrowly scoped, well-guarded credential access that is nonetheless sensitive.
llm_primary_threats: Scoped local credential file (.env) access for API keys

findings.title: Skill instructs reading API keys from a local .env file
findings.description: SKILL.md directs the agent to check environment variables and, if absent, read a `.env` file in the working directory for NCBI_API_KEY, CORE_API_KEY, S2_API_KEY, and OPENALEX_API_KEY. This is credential-file access, though it is narrowly scoped: the instructions explicitly limit reading to the four named variables, forbid loading the file wholesale into the environment or context, and forbid echoing keys. Scripts additionally redact api_key/email/mailto/tool values from emitted provenance URLs (_common.py redact_url). Risk is low and consistent with the stated purpose, but any .env read remains a sensitive operation worth noting.
findings.snippet: "If a key is absent there and a `.env` exists in the working directory, read **only** the four variables named in the table above — do not load the file wholesale into the environment or into your context, since it routinely holds unrelated secrets..."
findings.remediation: Prefer environment variables only, or require explicit user confirmation before reading a .env file. If .env access is retained, parse it with a strict allowlist parser in a bundled script rather than delegating the discipline to the model.

findings.title: Environment variable harvesting detected
findings.description: Script iterates through environment variables in skills/paper-lookup/scripts/paginate.py
findings.remediation: Remove environment variable collection unless explicitly required and documented

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This is a legitimate, unusually well-documented wrapper skill for the third-party Paperclip biomedical literature CLI. There are no scripts in the package, no hardcoded credentials, no obfuscation, no eval/exec patterns, and no data exfiltration to attacker-controlled endpoints; all network endpoints belong to the declared vendor (paperclip.gxl.ai) and the described behavior matches the manifest description and the declared allowed-tools (Bash, Read, Write). The skill notably contains explicit defensive guidance: it instructs the agent to treat all server-returned content (search snippets, paper full text, vendor docs) as data and never to follow instructions embedded in it, marks repositories and uploads as opt-in, and enumerates every command that causes data egress. Residual risks are inherent to the tool it wraps rather than malicious: a curl-to-bash installer with no checksum, an unversioned wheel plus an opportunistically self-updating binary, a documented path that writes vendor-controlled agent skill files into the project's .claude/skills directory, sourcing the whole .env into the child process environment, and egress/cookie-borrowing commands (upload/sync/share/fetch) that are gated behind explicit user request. No prompt injection, capability inflation, or deceptive behavior was detected.
llm_primary_threats: Supply chain risk: unverified remote install script and unversioned/self-updating binary
Transitive trust in remote vendor documentation and vendor-written agent skill files
Broad credential exposure via sourcing the entire .env into a third-party binary
Documented outbound data egress and browser-cookie-based fetching (user-gated)

findings.title: Remote installer piped directly to bash with no integrity verification
findings.description: The skill instructs the agent to install the CLI by fetching a remote shell script and executing it with the user's privileges. There is no checksum, signature, or version pin, so whatever the vendor endpoint serves at that moment is executed. The skill does mitigate this by telling the agent to confirm with the user first and by disclosing the absence of a checksum, but the pattern remains arbitrary remote code execution on the host.
findings.snippet: curl -fsSL https://paperclip.gxl.ai/install.sh | bash     # macOS/Linux; ~/.local/bin/paperclip
findings.remediation: Require explicit user confirmation before any install, prefer a pinned/versioned release artifact with a published SHA-256 checksum or signature, and recommend downloading + inspecting the script before execution rather than piping to bash.

findings.title: Auth prefix sources the entire .env file into the process environment
findings.description: The mandated auth prefix uses `set -a; . ./.env; set +a`, which exports every variable in the project's .env file — not just PAPERCLIP_API_KEY — into the environment of the paperclip binary on every single invocation. If the project .env holds unrelated secrets (cloud keys, DB passwords), they are exposed to a third-party, self-updating binary that makes network calls. Sourcing .env also executes any shell constructs it contains.
findings.snippet: [ -f .env ] && { set -a; . ./.env; set +a; }; paperclip <command>
findings.remediation: Prefer extracting only the needed variable, e.g. `PAPERCLIP_API_KEY=$(grep -m1 '^PAPERCLIP_API_KEY=' .env | cut -d= -f2-) paperclip <command>`, so unrelated secrets in .env are not exported to a third-party binary.

findings.title: Documented outbound data-egress and credential-borrowing commands
findings.description: The skill documents commands that move local content to the vendor or act outward with the user's identity: `upload`, `cp ~/path /clipboard/`, `sync add/run` (ongoing folder sync), `import ~/papers/` (recursive), `share FOLDER EMAIL`, and `fetch URL` which downloads using the user's browser cookies. These are legitimate features of the tool and the skill applies strong guardrails — an explicit egress table, 'never a whole home directory', 'never on your own initiative', repositories are opt-in, `--dry-run` first, and confirm folder and recipient with the user — but the capability set still warrants operator awareness.
findings.snippet:
| `paperclip fetch URL` | Uses the user's **browser cookies** to download as them |
| `paperclip share FOLDER EMAIL` | Grants another person access to the user's documents |
findings.remediation: Retain the explicit egress table and no-initiative rule; consider requiring per-invocation user confirmation for share/sync/fetch and enumerating exact file paths so no directory-wide upload can occur.

findings.title: Instruction to defer to remote vendor documentation output
findings.description: The skill tells the agent to run `paperclip skill` / `paperclip skills show <name>` for version-matched vendor documentation and to prefer the CLI's output over the local file where command syntax disagrees, and to load bundled domain workflows before multi-step analyses. This delegates part of the agent's operating instructions to remotely served, self-updating content. The risk is substantially mitigated by the skill's own rule 7, which explicitly instructs the agent to treat all server output as data, never to follow embedded instructions, and never to let returned content widen the task.
findings.snippet: Run `paperclip skill` for the vendor's version-matched documentation ... Where that output and this file disagree on *command syntax*, the CLI is newer
findings.remediation: Keep and strengthen rule 7; explicitly scope trust in remote documentation to command syntax only, and forbid executing any command string that first appears in server-returned content without user confirmation.

findings.title: Unversioned wheel URL and opportunistic self-updating binary
findings.description: The alternate install path installs an unversioned wheel URL (`https://paperclip.gxl.ai/paperclip.whl`), and the documentation notes that the CLI self-updates opportunistically mid-command. Both mean the executed code is not reproducible or pinnable, widening the supply-chain trust surface. The skill also correctly warns about a typosquatting hazard (an unrelated `paperclip` package exists on PyPI), which is a positive.
findings.snippet: uv pip install https://paperclip.gxl.ai/paperclip.whl ... The wheel URL is unversioned, so it resolves to whatever is current ... The CLI also self-updates opportunistically.
findings.remediation: Recommend installing a pinned, hash-verified release version and disabling opportunistic self-update in automated/agent contexts so the executing code is deterministic.

findings.title: Vendor-controlled skill files written into the agent's skill directory
findings.description: The skill documents a non-interactive invocation of `paperclip install` that writes vendor-supplied SKILL.md files into a project's agent configuration directory (e.g. `.claude/skills/paperclip/SKILL.md`), and `paperclip update` refreshes these installed agent skills. Because the content originates from a remote, self-updating service, this creates a path for third-party instructions to be injected into the agent's future instruction context without user review.
findings.snippet:
printf '1\n\n' | paperclip install --dir /path/to/project
# → writes /path/to/project/.claude/skills/paperclip/SKILL.md
findings.remediation: Require explicit user consent before writing any vendor-supplied skill/instruction files into agent configuration directories, and advise the user to review the written files (and any `paperclip update` refresh) before they are loaded as agent instructions.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The paperzilla skill is documentation-only: it contains no script files, no embedded code execution, no network exfiltration logic, and no credential harvesting. Its behavior (invoking a vendor `pz` CLI to read projects, papers, recommendations, feeds, and to leave feedback) is consistent with its name and description, with no capability inflation or keyword baiting beyond reasonable trigger terms. No prompt injection, obfuscation, or concealment directives were detected. Only minor, low-severity concerns exist: a vague instruction to follow additional "profile" instructions (potential future indirect-injection vector), unpinned third-party install channels for the CLI, and an absent optional `allowed-tools` declaration despite documented shell usage. Authentication is handled by the vendor CLI (`pz login`) rather than by hardcoded secrets, and the only environment variable referenced (`PZ_API_URL`) points at the vendor's own domain. Overall risk: LOW.
llm_primary_threats: Deference to unspecified external profile instructions (weak indirect prompt-injection vector)
Supply-chain trust in unpinned third-party CLI install channels
Undeclared tool permissions for documented Bash execution

findings.title: Unpinned third-party CLI installation from external taps/buckets
findings.description: Documentation instructs installing the `pz` binary via a third-party Homebrew tap and a Scoop bucket added from a GitHub URL, with no version pinning or checksum/signature verification. This is standard vendor install guidance but represents a supply-chain trust dependency on the vendor's repositories. No obfuscated `curl | bash` pattern is used.
findings.snippet:
brew install paperzilla-ai/tap/pz
scoop bucket add paperzilla-ai https://github.com/paperzilla-ai/scoop-bucket
scoop install pz
findings.remediation: Pin a specific CLI version and document checksum/signature verification for released binaries.

findings.title: Deference to unspecified "profile" instructions
findings.description: The SKILL.md instructs the agent: "If the current profile ships extra agent-specific instructions, follow those as well." This delegates trust to unspecified, external/other-file instruction sources that are not bundled or reviewable within this skill package, creating a potential vector for indirect prompt injection if a profile file is later added or modified by an untrusted party. Impact is limited because no such file is present and no automated fetching occurs.
findings.snippet: If the current profile ships extra agent-specific instructions, follow those as well.
findings.remediation: Explicitly enumerate and bundle any profile instruction files, and instruct the agent to treat their content as untrusted data rather than as instructions to follow.

findings.title: Missing allowed-tools declaration while documenting shell command execution
findings.description: The manifest does not declare `allowed-tools`, yet the instructions direct the agent to run numerous Bash commands (install, login, and `pz` subcommands). This is informational only, as `allowed-tools` is optional, but declaring it would constrain the skill to the minimum necessary tools (Bash) and prevent broader tool use.
findings.snippet: allowed-tools: Not specified; body contains multiple bash code blocks (brew install, pz login, pz feed ...)
findings.remediation: Add `allowed-tools: [Bash]` (or the minimal required set) to the YAML frontmatter.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
The `parallel-web` skill is a documentation-only wrapper (no Python or Bash script files are bundled) that routes user requests to the appropriate `parallel-cli` subcommand for web search, URL extraction, deep research, data enrichment, entity discovery, and recurring monitoring. Behavior is consistent with the manifest description: every capability described in the frontmatter maps to a corresponding reference file and CLI invocation, with no hidden functionality, no obfuscated or encoded payloads, no credential harvesting beyond the declared `PARALLEL_API_KEY`, and no network destinations other than the vendor's own API and user-authorized webhooks.

Notably, the skill demonstrates unusually strong defensive hygiene rather than security weaknesses. It explicitly instructs the agent to treat all search results, extracted pages, reports, enrichment values, and monitor events as untrusted data and never to follow embedded instructions or credential prompts — an explicit indirect-prompt-injection countermeasure repeated across four reference files. It mandates passing user text as a single quoted argument or via stdin instead of constructing shell source, forbids concatenating raw user text into JSON or shell commands, and requires validating CLI-returned task IDs against expected prefixes (`trun_`, `tgrp_`, `findall_`/`frun_`, `mon_`) while rejecting whitespace and shell metacharacters — meaningful command-injection mitigation. Availability risk is bounded: polling is explicitly capped at three attempts with `--timeout 540` and unbounded polling loops are prohibited. Destructive or state-mutating operations (monitor create/update/trigger/cancel) require explicit user authorization and re-verification, and cost-amplifying tiers (deep research, high match limits) require explicit user intent plus cost warnings. Secret handling is disciplined: no key echoing, no bulk `.env` inspection, no credentials in webhook URLs.

Only three low-severity, largely informational observations remain: the optional `allowed-tools` field is absent even though the skill relies entirely on shell execution; setup performs third-party package installation (correctly pinned to `==0.7.1` in an isolated uv environment, though the upgrade command is necessarily unpinned) and suggests a PATH modification; and the skill legitimately handles a secret API key while uploading user-supplied rows to a third-party service and writing artifacts to disk. None of these constitute malicious behavior. Overall the package appears benign and well-engineered from a security standpoint.

findings.title: Skill requires a secret API key and can write result artifacts to disk
findings.description: The skill consumes `PARALLEL_API_KEY`, may perform interactive/device login, sends user-supplied query text and user-supplied CSV/JSON rows to Parallel's third-party API, and can write result files (`-o research-report`, `--target enriched.csv`). It can also register outbound webhooks to arbitrary HTTPS endpoints. All of this is inherent to the stated purpose and is accompanied by strong guardrails: no key printing/logging, no `.env` enumeration beyond checking for the key name, webhook must be user-authorized and credential-free, previews must avoid sensitive input fields, and artifacts should go to a user-specified or temp path rather than the repo root. No hardcoded secrets and no exfiltration to attacker-controlled infrastructure were found; this is noted for data-flow awareness only.
findings.snippet:
Do not print, log, or include `PARALLEL_API_KEY` in command arguments or output.
Do not inspect an entire `.env` file; ... never display its value.
--webhook "https://example.com/parallel-events" ... Send events only to a user-authorized HTTPS endpoint. Do not place credentials in the webhook URL.
findings.remediation: No change required for safety, but confirm with the user before uploading local CSV/JSON files or registering webhooks, and continue to source the key from the environment/credential store only.

findings.title: Third-party package installation from PyPI (version-pinned) and PATH modification
findings.description: Setup instructs installing `parallel-web-tools[cli]==0.7.1` via `uv tool install`, an upgrade path via `uv tool upgrade parallel-web-tools` (which is unpinned by design), and adding `~/.local/bin` to PATH. The initial install is correctly pinned to an exact version and installed in an isolated uv tool environment, which is good practice; residual supply-chain risk stems only from trusting the upstream package/registry and from the unpinned upgrade command. No integrity hash or repository provenance is provided.
findings.snippet:
uv tool install "parallel-web-tools[cli]==0.7.1"
uv tool upgrade parallel-web-tools
If `parallel-cli` is not found after install, add `~/.local/bin` to PATH.
findings.remediation: Keep the exact version pin, document the expected publisher/repository for `parallel-web-tools`, and require explicit user confirmation before running install/upgrade commands or modifying PATH.

findings.title: No allowed-tools declared for a skill that instructs Bash command execution
findings.description: The YAML manifest omits the optional `allowed-tools` field even though the skill's entire workflow depends on executing shell commands (`parallel-cli ...`, `uv tool install`). This is informational only: the skill does not declare restrictions and therefore does not violate any, but explicitly declaring Bash (and no more) would make the required privileges auditable and prevent silent scope creep.
findings.snippet: allowed-tools: Not specified; body contains numerous ```bash blocks (e.g. `parallel-cli login`, `uv tool install "parallel-web-tools[cli]==0.7.1"`)
findings.remediation: Add an explicit `allowed-tools` entry (e.g. `[Bash, Read, Write]`) to the frontmatter to document and bound the privileges the skill needs.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
The `pathml` skill is a well-documented, defensively engineered research-support skill for computational pathology workflows. All four bundled Python CLIs (`plan_pipeline.py`, `plan_inference.py`, `image_qc.py`, `slide_manifest.py`, plus shared `_common.py`) are network-free, dependency-light, and implement strong input hardening: URL rejection, symlink-component rejection, root-confinement (`relative_to` checks), regular-file/size caps, strict JSON parsing with duplicate-key and NaN/Infinity rejection, bounded row/node/edge/pixel counts, allowlisted file suffixes, atomic writes with 0o600 permissions and no-clobber-by-default behavior. No `eval`, `exec`, `os.system`, `subprocess`, `pickle`, `requests`/`urllib`, or credential-path access appears anywhere in the code. The only `os.environ`-adjacent usage is `os.sys.stderr` for error printing — there is no environment-variable harvesting and no outbound network capability, so the static pre-scan flags for "env var exfiltration" and "cross-file exfiltration chain" are false positives (they appear to be triggered by the presence of `os` imports plus documentation strings containing HTTPS URLs of upstream PathML/Hugging Face endpoints).

The SKILL.md body contains no prompt-injection, instruction-override, concealment, or role-redefinition language. To the contrary, it repeatedly reinforces safe behavior: a no-network default with an explicit user-consent gate before any download-capable PathML class is instantiated, warnings that PathML's `.pt`/pickle/h5path loaders execute code and must never be pointed at untrusted artifacts, explicit prohibition of Python dynamic evaluation, module-shadowing warnings, PHI/de-identification handling rules, and a clear non-clinical-use disclaimer. Declared `allowed-tools` (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob) are consistent with actual behavior (local file reads, bounded local writes, CLI invocation). Installation guidance uses a pinned version (`pathml==3.0.5`) via `uv`, discourages `pathml[all]`, and documents platform prerequisites — good supply-chain hygiene. External HTTPS references are citations/primary sources for human review, not instructions to fetch and execute remote content, so they do not constitute transitive-trust delegation.

Minor, non-security observations: the skill declares `.py` files that use a bare `from _common import ...` (requires execution from the scripts directory), and several referenced doc paths listed by the scanner (`assets/*.md`, `templates/*.md`, `pathml.py`) do not exist — the `pathml.py` "reference" is actually a warning in SKILL.md about not naming local files after modules, not a bundled file. Neither is a security threat. No findings warranting a severity rating were identified.

The pathogen-variant-surveillance skill is a well-engineered, standard-library-only Python toolkit that queries public GenSpectrum LAPIS APIs for viral genomic surveillance data. No malicious behavior was found. There is no eval/exec/os.system, no subprocess usage, no shell invocation, no credential or filesystem harvesting, no environment-variable reading, no hardcoded secrets, no base64/obfuscated payloads, and no exfiltration of local data \u2014 all network traffic is outbound HTTP GET to documented public scientific endpoints (lapis.cov-spectrum.org, lapis.genspectrum.org, lapis.pathoplexus.org, raw.githubusercontent.com), with only query parameters derived from user CLI arguments. File writes are limited to an explicit user-specified -o/--output path, consistent with the declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash). The SKILL.md body contains no prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, or safety-bypass language; it instead enforces conservative epidemiological practice and explicitly disclaims clinical/public-health guidance. Retries are bounded (MAX_ATTEMPTS=3 with linear backoff) and loops are bounded, so no DoS/compute-exhaustion concern. The long keyword-rich description is proportionate to a genuinely narrow, domain-specific skill and does not constitute capability inflation. Behavior matches the manifest across all components. The only observations are two low-severity, already-documented and already-mitigated external-data trust considerations.

findings.title: Unpinned fetch of external pango-designation data from raw.githubusercontent.com
findings.description: The client fetches alias_key.json and lineage_notes.txt from the master branch of the cov-lineages/pango-designation GitHub repository at run time, deliberately unpinned. This is documented and justified (withdrawals/redesignations must be current), and the content is parsed as data only — never executed. Residual risk is that content of an upstream repository could change and influence agent-visible output. Mitigated by provenance printing of the ETag blob SHA and by sanitize() stripping control characters from remote text before rendering.
findings.snippet: PANGO_ALIAS_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cov-lineages/pango-designation/master/pango_designation/alias_key.json"
findings.remediation: No change required for intended use. Optionally allow an opt-in pinned tag/commit for reproducible offline audits, and continue printing the blob SHA provenance line.

findings.title: Remote LAPIS instance content rendered into agent-visible output (user-supplied --base-url)
findings.description: Scripts accept an arbitrary --base-url and print remote field names, lineage labels, and HTTP error 'detail' strings into stdout/stderr that an agent reads. A hostile deployment could return text shaped like instructions. The skill explicitly documents this risk and mitigates it: sanitize() strips all C0/C1 control characters and collapses whitespace, responses are parsed as JSON data and never executed, and the reference file warns to point --base-url only at trusted deployments. Residual risk is limited to plain-text content that an agent might read as guidance.
findings.snippet: "Safety: this output is read by an agent, so remote text is untrusted input. Stripping control characters and collapsing line breaks stops a hostile or malformed instance from forging rows..."
findings.remediation: Consider restricting --base-url to an allowlist of known hosts by default (with an explicit --allow-untrusted-instance flag), and label remote-derived text blocks as untrusted data in output.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The `pathway-enrichment` skill is a legitimate bioinformatics helper for over-representation and GSEA analyses using gseapy/g:Profiler. Review of the SKILL.md body, the single Python script (`scripts/run_enrichment.py`), and the three bundled reference files found no prompt injection, no instruction-override or concealment language, no credential access (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, env harvesting), no hardcoded secrets, and no obfuscated or encoded payloads. Network activity is limited to well-known, documented public bioinformatics services (Enrichr, MSigDB, g:Profiler, Biomart) and is disclosed in the instructions and script docstring — it is intrinsic to the stated purpose, not exfiltration. File I/O is scoped to user-specified input files and an explicit --outdir. The static analyzer hint 'MDBLOCK_PYTHON_EVAL_EXEC' appears to be a false positive: no `eval()`, `exec()`, `os.system`, `subprocess`, or shell interpolation exists in any code block or script; the only dynamic constructs are pandas/gseapy API calls and argparse handling. Description and declared capabilities match actual behavior, and the keyword-rich description is domain-appropriate rather than keyword baiting. Only minor hygiene issues were identified (unpinned dependencies, absent optional manifest metadata). Overall the package appears safe to use.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This is the upstream Anthropic `pdf` skill (version 1.2, source github.com/anthropics/skills) and it appears benign. The 'not found' referenced files (reportlab.py, pypdf.py, pdfplumber.py, pdf2image.py, pytesseract.py) are Python library import names misparsed as local file references, not missing bundled resources. scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The peer-review skill appears benign and unusually well-scoped. All seven bundled Python scripts (`_common.py`, `validate_review_intake.py`, `select_reporting_guidelines.py`, `validate_claim_evidence.py`, `audit_statistics_reproducibility.py`, `audit_citations.py`, `generate_review_scaffold.py`, `lint_review.py`) use only the Python standard library and contain no network calls (no requests/urllib/socket/http), no subprocess or os.system invocation, no eval/exec/compile, no pickle/marshal, no environment-variable or credential access (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, .env), no hardcoded secrets, and no obfuscated or encoded payloads. Data flow is strictly local: bounded JSON/CSV/Markdown inputs are read from explicitly supplied paths and reports are written to stdout or an explicitly named local file. The shared helper module implements defensive controls that reduce rather than create risk: 4 MiB input cap, 5,000-row CSV cap, 12,000-char cell cap, list-size caps, UTF-8-only decoding with NUL rejection, duplicate JSON key and duplicate CSV header rejection, symlink rejection for both inputs and outputs, refusal to overwrite existing outputs without --force, and atomic writes with 0o600 permissions. These bounds also mitigate resource-exhaustion/DoS concerns. Report minimization is intentional and consistently implemented — outputs emit IDs, counts, rule codes, and line numbers rather than manuscript, claim, or reference prose, which limits confidential-content leakage into logs or downstream contexts. No prompt injection, jailbreak, role redefinition, concealment directive ('do not tell the user'), or system-prompt-extraction language was found in SKILL.md or any reference file, in English or any other language. The instruction body is safety-additive: it establishes an explicit authorization gate before unpublished material is read, forbids sending confidential content to external services, forbids reading .env files/API keys/credentials, forbids network/LLM/image calls from bundled tools, forbids impersonating reviewers or editors, forbids fabricating findings or announcing editorial decisions, and requires human accountability. The `lint_review.py` regexes actively detect impersonation, editorial-decision, and false-execution claims. The only external URLs in the package are informational citations in `assets/source_ledger.csv`, `assets/reporting_guidelines.json`, and reference markdown; no script fetches them, and no instruction tells the agent to retrieve and follow remote content, so there is no indirect-prompt-injection or transitive-trust path. The description is specific to peer review and matches actual behavior, with no keyword baiting, brand impersonation, activation-priority manipulation, or capability inflation. All file reads are of internal, bundled assets (normal, expected behavior) or user-supplied local paths passed as explicit CLI arguments. Findings are limited to three LOW-severity hygiene items: missing optional `allowed-tools` metadata, a handful of documented-but-absent asset paths, and a self-attested security-validation document whose claims cannot be independently verified from the package (though the shipped code is consistent with them). No CRITICAL, HIGH, or MEDIUM issues were identified.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The `pennylane` skill is a documentation/reference package for the legitimate PennyLane quantum computing framework. findings.title: Documentation examples may cause heavy local compute usage

estimate_resources(n_qubits=20, depth=100)

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
This skill is a documentation/reference package for the "Pi" terminal coding agent. It contains 13 markdown files and no executable scripts (no .py, .sh, or other runnable code). The SKILL.md body is a routing table that maps user intents to internal reference files bundled with the package — reading these internal files is normal, expected skill behavior.

No prompt injection, jailbreak, instruction-override, concealment, or role-redefinition language was found in any file (checked language-agnostically). There is no data exfiltration, no credential harvesting, no hardcoded secrets, and no network calls performed by the skill itself. Provider environment-variable names and auth file paths (e.g. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, ~/.pi/agent/auth.json) appear only as legitimate configuration documentation, with placeholder values such as "sk-ant-..." — not real keys or read-and-send patterns.

The pre-scan flag "MDBLOCK_PYTHON_EVAL_EXEC" appears to be a false positive: the fenced code blocks in these files are TypeScript/JSON/bash documentation samples (e.g. `execute(toolCallId, params)` tool-handler signatures, `pi.exec(command, args)` API descriptions, `eval "$(grep '^alias ' ~/.zshrc)"` in a documented shell-alias setting). None of it is skill-executed Python eval/exec, and none constructs commands from untrusted input within the skill.

Cross-component consistency is good: the manifest description matches the bundled content, and the skill explicitly includes a "Safety Defaults" section warning that Pi is not sandboxed, that extensions/packages/skills run with full process permissions, that secrets should not be stored in project files, and that untrusted repos should be isolated via container/VM. That is security-positive framing rather than a threat.

Residual concerns are minor and informational: an unusually broad activation description, a large number of unresolved assets/ and templates/ references, and documented (not executed) unpinned install commands. Overall this package appears benign.

findings.title: Very broad skill description increases activation surface
findings.description: The skill description is unusually long and enumerates many keywords (installing, configuring, providers, models, SDK, RPC, MCP, web search, subagents, video understanding, etc.). This is legitimate for a documentation-reference skill covering an entire product, but it broadens discovery/activation triggers considerably. No deceptive claims were found: the described purpose (Pi documentation reference) matches the actual bundled content, which is purely markdown documentation.
findings.snippet: description: Build with and use Pi, the minimal terminal coding harness. Use for installing Pi, configuring providers/models/settings/environment variables, creating Pi skills/extensions/packages/themes/prompt templates, embedding Pi through the SDK, integrating over RPC or JSON event streams, parsing sessions, running local models through the llama.cpp router, ... pi-web-access (web search, fetching, video understanding).
findings.remediation: Optionally narrow the description to the core intent ("reference documentation for the Pi terminal coding agent") to reduce unnecessary activation, and keep the detailed capability list in the instruction body.

findings.title: Documented install/package commands pull unpinned remote code (informational)
findings.description: The skill body and reference files document standard Pi installation and package-management commands that fetch and execute remote code without version pinning, e.g. `npm install -g --ignore-scripts @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent`, `pi install npm:pi-subagents`, and `curl -fsSL https://pi.dev/install.sh | sh`. These are the vendor's own documented commands and are quoted as documentation rather than executed by the skill, but an agent following them would install unpinned third-party code with full user permissions. The documentation does include mitigations (`--ignore-scripts`, explicit warnings that packages run with full system access, and a security/containerization section).
findings.snippet:
npm install -g --ignore-scripts @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent
pi install npm:pi-subagents
curl -fsSL https://pi.dev/install.sh | sh
findings.remediation: Recommend pinned versions (e.g. `npm:pkg@x.y.z`) in the documented examples and require explicit user confirmation before the agent runs any install command.

findings.description: The static analyzer resolved a large number of referenced paths under assets/ and templates/ that are not present in the package (e.g. assets/settings.md, templates/rpc.md). Only the references/*.md files actually exist. Missing files are a documentation-integrity issue: if an agent attempts to read them it will fail, and future placement of files at those paths would be loaded without review. scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The pkpd-modeling skill appears benign and technically well-engineered. All nine scripts plus the two shared modules (_models.py, _common.py) perform purely local numerical computation with numpy/scipy: no network calls (no requests/urllib/socket), no subprocess/os.system/eval/exec, no environment-variable or credential access, no file writes, no reads of sensitive paths (~/.aws, ~/.ssh), no base64/hex-encoded blobs or other obfuscation, and no dynamic dependency installation. File input is limited to user-specified CSV/TSV paths or stdin via a defensive read_table() helper, and argument parsing uses argparse with validation that raises InputError rather than interpolating user data into shells or code. The SKILL.md body contains no prompt-injection, role-redefinition, concealment, or safety-bypass language; behaviour matches the declared description, and the declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are not exceeded by the code (scripts only read input files and write to stdout/stderr). The compatibility claim of 'no network access' is consistent with the code. Bundled reference documents contain only domain guidance with no embedded instructions to the agent. Only minor, non-exploitable issues were noted: a keyword-dense activation description, several unresolved internal reference paths, and the inherent need for clinical oversight of dosing output (already explicitly disclaimed).

findings.title: Very keyword-dense activation description
findings.description: The YAML description embeds ~40 explicit trigger keywords ("pharmacokinetics", "NONMEM", "Monolix", "bioequivalence", "MABEL", "MIPD", etc.). All terms are legitimate and tightly scoped to pharmacometrics, so this is not deceptive capability inflation, but the density increases the chance of unintended activation for tangential queries. No brand impersonation or over-broad "general assistant" claims were found.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
The polars-bio skill is a documentation-only skill that teaches usage of the legitimate open-source polars-bio Python library for genomic interval operations and bioinformatics file I/O. No executable scripts are included (no .py or .sh payloads shipped), and all provided content — SKILL.md plus references/interval_operations.md, references/file_io.md, references/sql_processing.md, references/pileup_operations.md — consists of accurate API documentation, parameter tables, and code examples consistent with the stated purpose.

Security review results:
- Manifest: name and description match observed behavior; no keyword baiting, brand impersonation, or over-broad capability claims. allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) is consistent with a skill that installs a package and reads/writes genomic files; nothing in the content exceeds these declarations.
- Instructions: no prompt injection, no instruction overrides, no concealment ("do not tell the user"), no role redefinition, no safety-bypass language, in English or any other language.
- Scripts: none present. The pre-scan hint "BEHAVIOR_EVAL_SUBPROCESS: eval/exec combined with subprocess" could not be corroborated anywhere in the delivered content — there are no eval/exec/os.system/subprocess calls, no shell pipelines, no base64/hex blobs, and no obfuscation. The only shell command documented is a version-pinned `uv pip install "polars-bio==0.31.0"`. This appears to be a false positive (likely triggered by SQL/DataFusion "execute query" wording or generic keyword matching in unresolved referenced filenames such as polars.py / polars_bio.py, which are absent).
- Data flow: no network exfiltration, no reads of ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, .env files, no environment-variable harvesting, no telemetry endpoints, no hardcoded secrets or API keys. Cloud credential use is only the standard, disclosed SDK behavior triggered by user-supplied s3://, gs://, or az:// paths.
- Behavioral/autonomy: no unbounded loops, no "retry until success", no cross-session memory bridging, no over-collection (no home-directory walks), no read→send tool chaining, and no instruction to follow content fetched from external URLs.

Residual concerns are minor and non-exploitable: an external (though pinned) PyPI dependency, standard ambient cloud credential usage, and several documentation references pointing to files that are not shipped. scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This is the official Anthropic-authored `pptx` skill (vendored from github.com/anthropics/skills), and the analysis found no malicious behavior. All scripts perform exactly what the manifest and instructions claim: unpacking/repacking OOXML ZIP packages, duplicating slides with correct package bookkeeping, removing orphaned parts, rendering thumbnails via LibreOffice + pdftoppm, and validating slide/chart XML against XSD schemas. There is no network egress, no credential or environment harvesting, no eval/exec of dynamic input, no obfuscated or encoded payloads, and no hardcoded secrets. The instruction body contains no prompt injection, no concealment directives, and no attempt to override agent safety behavior — it is entirely domain guidance on PowerPoint generation, design, and QA. Notably, the code shows above-average security hygiene: `safe_extract()` rejects symlink archive entries and zip-slip paths, XML is parsed with `defusedxml` to block XXE/billion-laughs, `opc_target()` rejects relationship targets that escape the package or use external/URI schemes, `rezip()` writes atomically via mkstemp+os.replace with preserved permissions, the soffice environment is built from an explicit allowlist specifically so agent API keys are not leaked into converter subprocesses, and `clean.py` refuses to delete when parsing looks to have failed. Two low-severity informational items are noted: an aggressively broad activation description, and the runtime gcc-compiled LD_PRELOAD shim used to work around blocked AF_UNIX sockets (documented, self-hardened against a prior predictable-path issue, but an inherently privileged pattern). Neither indicates malicious intent. Missing `allowed-tools` and `compatibility` fields are optional per spec; the skill does declare version, author, license, and upstream source.

findings.title: Very broad, keyword-heavy activation description
findings.description: The frontmatter description is unusually aggressive about activation ('Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way', 'Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation"', 'regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward'). This is keyword baiting that maximizes activation frequency. In this case the scope stays within PPTX handling and is consistent with the bundled scripts, so the risk is limited to over-activation rather than capability inflation into unrelated domains.
findings.snippet: "Trigger whenever the user mentions \"deck,\" \"slides,\" \"presentation,\" or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward."
findings.remediation: Narrow the description to concrete file-format tasks and remove blanket 'always trigger' phrasing so skill selection stays proportional to the user's actual request.

findings.title: Runtime C compilation and LD_PRELOAD injection into soffice subprocess
findings.description: scripts/office/soffice.py writes a C source file at runtime, compiles it with gcc, and injects the resulting shared object into every LibreOffice subprocess via LD_PRELOAD. The shim hooks socket/listen/accept/close and calls _exit(0). This is legitimate, documented sandbox workaround code, and the implementation is defensive: it compiles into a fresh 0700 mkdtemp directory (explicitly to avoid a previously-noted predictable /tmp path hijack), removes the .c after compiling, and registers atexit cleanup. Flagged as informational only because runtime code compilation plus library preloading is an intrinsically high-privilege pattern that reviewers should be aware of.
findings.snippet: shim_dir = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="lo-shim-")) ... subprocess.run(["gcc", "-shared", "-fPIC", "-o", str(so), str(src), "-ldl"], check=True, ...) ... env["LD_PRELOAD"] = str(shim)
findings.remediation: No action strictly required; the temp-dir hardening and env allowlist already mitigate the known risks. Optionally ship a prebuilt, integrity-verified shim or gate compilation behind an explicit opt-in flag.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The pptx-posters skill is a well-engineered, defensively written local document-generation and auditing toolkit and appears benign. Review of all seven CLIs plus the two shared modules found no prompt injection, jailbreak language, role redefinition, concealment directives, or safety-bypass instructions in SKILL.md or the reference markdown; the instruction body is a fail-closed procedural workflow that repeatedly demands human author approval and refuses to fabricate content. No network activity exists anywhere in the code: there are no imports of requests, urllib, socket, or http, no subprocess/os.system/eval/exec/pickle/marshal usage, no environment-variable or credential harvesting (no ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, ~/.netrc, os.environ reads), and no hardcoded secrets or obfuscated/base64 payloads. File access is tightly scoped: resolve_local_asset() rejects absolute paths, URI schemes, backslashes, and '..' segments and enforces containment under the manifest's own directory via resolve()+relative_to(); checked_input_file() rejects symlinks and non-regular files with size caps; checked_output_file()/commit_temp_file() refuse to overwrite existing destinations and create mode-0600 temp files in the destination directory. XML parsing rejects DTD/ENTITY declarations before parse (XXE/billion-laughs mitigation), ZIP handling never calls extract/extractall and pre-bounds the central directory, and the package inspector explicitly rejects macros, ActiveX, OLE, embedded parts, and all External-TargetMode relationships. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Bash, Glob, Grep, Python) are consistent with observed behavior (local file reads/writes plus a documented uv pip install of exactly pinned dependencies python-pptx==1.0.2, Pillow==12.3.0, lxml==6.1.1 — pinned, from PyPI, no direct GitHub installs, no typosquat indicators). The description is narrowly scoped with no keyword baiting, brand impersonation, activation-priority manipulation, or capability inflation, and it matches actual behavior. Only two LOW informational findings remain: documented-but-bounded compute consumption limits, and a set of reference paths in SKILL.md that do not resolve to bundled files.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
The protocolsio-integration skill is a defensively engineered, read-oriented API client for protocols.io. Across all five Python modules the security posture is unusually strong and consistent with the manifest claims:

- Network: only HTTPS GET requests, hard host allowlist (protocols.io, www.protocols.io, and a strict `<subdomain>.protocols.io` regex), port restricted to 443, no URL credentials, redirects explicitly rejected via a custom NoRedirectHandler, and ambient proxies disabled (ProxyHandler({})). Network activity requires an explicit `--execute` flag; default mode only prints a plan. There are no external/attacker-controlled domains anywhere.
- Credentials: only one named environment variable (PROTOCOLS_IO_ACCESS_TOKEN) is read; there is no full-environment enumeration, no .env loading, no ~/.aws or ~/.ssh access, and no hardcoded secrets. Tokens are never echoed — validate_auth_config.py returns presence booleans only, and plan output substitutes a placeholder for the Authorization header. Sensitive-key redaction is applied to both payloads and remote responses.
- Execution safety: no eval/exec/os.system/subprocess, no shell invocation, no dynamic imports, no deserialization of pickles, and no obfuscation or encoded blobs. Only the Python standard library is used, matching the compatibility statement; there is no pip/npm installation or supply-chain fetch.
- Filesystem: all input/output paths are constrained to the CWD with parent-traversal and symlink rejection, output files must not already exist, and PDF bytes are written with 0600 permissions via O_EXCL. Local file reads are size-capped.
- Resource bounds: page/item/byte/depth/timeout caps everywhere, retries limited to 0–2 for idempotent GETs only, Retry-After capped at 30s, and the linked-step traversal uses a visited-set guard so no unbounded loop exists.
- Mutation handling: plan_write_request.py has no network or execution path at all; it validates payload shapes strictly against documented field allowlists, redacts credential-like fields, and requires a confirmation phrase that still does not execute.
- Prompt-injection posture: the instructions and reference docs repeatedly and explicitly instruct the agent to treat protocol text, comments, filenames, links, signed upload fields, and error messages as untrusted data and never obey embedded instructions. This is defensive guidance, not injection. No instruction-override, concealment, role-redefinition, or safety-bypass language appears in any language.
- Manifest consistency: declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Python) match observed behavior — the scripts read local JSON, write a PDF output file, and run as Python; no Bash execution occurs. The description accurately narrows activation to protocols.io tasks and does not use keyword baiting or over-broad capability claims.

Only a trivial documentation-consistency observation was noted. No malicious behavior, data exfiltration, injection, obfuscation, or capability inflation was found.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This is a well-constructed, defense-oriented documentation and tooling skill for PufferLib. All seven bundled Python CLIs are standard-library only, offline, deterministic, and bounded: no network libraries, no subprocess/shell execution, no eval/exec/dynamic imports, no pickle or torch.load, no os.environ reads, and no credential file access. Security controls are unusually strong and appear genuine: resolve_local_path() enforces root containment and rejects symlinks and traversal; inspect_checkpoint.py opens files with O_NOFOLLOW, requires a regular file, and hashes/classifies bytes without deserialization; _common.py implements strict JSON parsing (duplicate-key and non-finite rejection), bounded integer validation, slug-only identifiers that explicitly reject dotted import paths, and secret_key_paths() that rejects credential-bearing config keys. Resource use is capped everywhere (steps, envs, workers, repeats, file sizes) and multiprocessing deliberately excludes 'fork'. SKILL.md instructions contain no prompt injection, no concealment directives, no instruction overrides, and no safety-bypass language; the guidance consistently pushes toward pinned versions, verified digests, sandboxed builds, and explicit opt-in for external logging. The declared allowed-tools (Read, Bash, Grep, Python) are consistent with observed behavior — scripts only read local files under an explicit root and write to stdout. Referenced external URLs are legitimate upstream sources (PyPI, GitHub PufferAI, official docs, arXiv/OpenReview) cited as documentation, not fetched or executed by any script. Several referenced-file paths reported as 'not found' (templates/*, assets/*, pufferlib.py) are inventory artifacts of link scanning, not real dangling dependencies of the instructions. The pre-scan behavioral alerts about env-var exfiltration are assessed as false positives. No CRITICAL, HIGH, or MEDIUM threats identified.

This pydicom skill appears benign and unusually security-conscious. All seven helper CLIs are local-only: there are no network calls (no requests/urllib/socket/subprocess), no eval/exec, no shell invocation, no environment-variable or credential harvesting, and no hardcoded secrets. The pre-scan flag BEHAVIOR_EVAL_SUBPROCESS could not be substantiated — no eval(), exec(), os.system(), or subprocess usage exists anywhere in the provided code; it appears to be a false positive (likely triggered by identifiers such as 'inspect', 'importlib.metadata', or 'process_file'). scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The `pyhealth` skill is a legitimate, documentation-oriented reference package for building clinical ML pipelines with the open-source PyHealth library. scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
The pytdc skill is a well-engineered, defensively written wrapper around the legitimate PyTDC (Therapeutics Data Commons) Python package. No malicious behavior was found.

Manifest consistency: name, description, compatibility notes, and allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) match the actual behavior — the scripts read/write only relative workspace paths and are invoked via Bash/uv. Instructions: No prompt injection, role redefinition, safety-bypass, or concealment language. Scripts: All five Python files use standard-library-only helpers plus lazy imports of tdc. The static analyzer flag MDBLOCK_PYTHON_EVAL_EXEC appears to be a false positive — no eval(), exec(), compile(), os.system(), or subprocess call with interpolated input exists in any reference file; the likely trigger is benign token overlap (e.g., 'zot.everything(', 'execute'/'exceeds' text, or Zotero 'exports' snippets). scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The qiskit skill is a well-structured, documentation-heavy technical reference for building and executing quantum circuits with Qiskit 2.x and IBM Quantum Runtime. No prompt injection, jailbreak language, concealment directives, role redefinition, or safety-bypass instructions were found in SKILL.md or any bundled reference file. The three bundled Python scripts were reviewed in full: check_environment.py only reads installed distribution metadata and imports modules (no network, no credential access); run_local_primitives.py performs purely local statevector simulation with bounded argument validation (shots capped at 1,000,000, finite-float checks, positive-qubit checks) which mitigates compute-exhaustion risk; inspect_runtime.py performs read-only, authenticated queries to IBM Quantum using locally saved credentials and never submits a job. There is no eval/exec, no os.system or subprocess with interpolated input, no base64/hex obfuscation, no hardcoded secrets, no filesystem traversal of the home directory, no reading of ~/.aws or ~/.ssh, and no outbound transmission of local data to third-party or attacker-controlled endpoints. Error handling in inspect_runtime.py deliberately avoids echoing request payloads or account details, and the documentation repeatedly and correctly instructs against printing, logging, committing, or serializing API keys, saved-account files, headers, or environments. Referenced files are all internal to the package; a large number of listed template/asset paths and bare module names (templates/*.md, assets/*.md, qiskit.py, qiskit_ibm_runtime.py) are not present, which appears to be reference-extraction noise from import statements rather than an attempt to load external or untrusted content. No external URLs are fetched or executed; documentation links point to official IBM Quantum, PyPI, and Qiskit GitHub domains and are cited as human-readable references only. The description accurately matches actual behavior with no keyword baiting, brand impersonation, or capability inflation. Residual observations are limited to inherent, well-documented risks: legitimate use of IBM Quantum credentials and network access, PyPI installation of version-pinned official packages, and an unspecified (optional) allowed-tools field. scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment:
The `qutip` skill is a well-engineered, defensive scientific-computing skill for quantum dynamics simulation with QuTiP 5.3.0. No security threats were identified.

Analysis details:
- **Manifest**: Name, description, and compatibility notes accurately reflect behavior (local simulation/planning CLIs, no network use). `allowed-tools` is not specified, which is optional per spec and only informational here; the skill's actual behavior (local Python execution and local file read/write of JSON) is consistent with its stated purpose.
- **SKILL.md body**: Contains only technical physics/numerics guidance. No prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, safety-bypass language, or instructions to fetch/execute external content. It explicitly warns *against* risky patterns: "Do not create coefficient source strings from user input", "This skill never uses Python dynamic-code execution", and "Do not load untrusted QuTiP object/result files because object serialization can execute code."
- **Scripts**: All five CLIs plus `_common.py` use `argparse` with constrained `choices`, strict bounds validation (`finite_float`, `bounded_int`, `bounded_dimensions`), and raise `CliError` on violations. There is no `eval`, `exec`, `compile`, `pickle`, `subprocess`, `os.system`, or any network/socket/HTTP usage. JSON parsing is hardened: `parse_constant` rejects NaN/Infinity, `object_pairs_hook` rejects duplicate keys, unknown keys are rejected via `validate_keys`, and output serialization uses `allow_nan=False` with a size cap.
- **File I/O safety**: `checked_input_file`/`checked_output_file` reject `://` URLs, reject symlinks, require regular files, enforce a 1 MiB input cap and 8 MiB report cap, restrict suffixes to `.json`, require an explicit `--force` to overwrite, and write atomically via `mkstemp` + `os.chmod(0o600)` + `os.replace`. No home-directory traversal, no credential paths (`~/.aws`, `~/.ssh`), no environment-variable harvesting, no hardcoded secrets.
- **Resource limits**: Explicit caps on Hilbert dimension (64), subsystems (8), model objects (32), time points (5001), trajectories (2000), sweep runs (6), and total sweep trajectories (4000) mitigate compute-exhaustion risk. No unbounded loops or retry logic.
- **Dependencies**: Documented installs are exactly pinned (`qutip==5.3.0`, `qutip-qip==0.4.2`, etc.), `load_qutip()` verifies the installed version matches the pin, and the skill explicitly advises against installing the unreleased `qutip-cupy` from Git. No typosquatting indicators; all packages are the official QuTiP-organization distributions.
- **Referenced files**: The five `references/*.md` files that were provided are internal to the package and contain only legitimate technical documentation with no embedded instructions to the agent and no hidden payloads. The scanner-listed `assets/*`, `templates/*`, and `qutip.py` paths are false positives from substring matching of reference filenames; the SKILL.md only references `references/*.md`. Missing files are a documentation-hygiene non-issue, not a security concern.
- **Cross-component consistency**: Every documented script exists, and each script's behavior matches its described purpose. No hidden capabilities, no tool chaining toward exfiltration (read→send), no cross-context bridging, and no over-collection.

Recommendation: No remediation required. Optionally, the author could declare `allowed-tools: [Read, Write, Bash, Python]` for explicitness and add the missing `references/` files if any links are stale.

The `rdkit` skill is a legitimate cheminformatics documentation-and-example package. The SKILL.md body contains no prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, or safety-bypass language; it is purely technical guidance on RDKit APIs. All three bundled Python scripts (molecular_properties.py, similarity_search.py, substructure_filter.py) are self-contained, use only RDKit/argparse/csv/pathlib, and perform exactly what the description claims: parse molecules, compute descriptors, compute fingerprint similarity, and filter by SMARTS. There is no network activity, no environment-variable or credential access (no ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, no os.environ), no subprocess/os.system/eval/exec, no base64/obfuscated payloads, and no filesystem traversal beyond user-specified input/output paths. Declared `allowed-tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash` is consistent with the scripts' behavior (reading molecule files, writing CSV/SDF/SMILES outputs, running CLI scripts); no violation detected. Referenced files resolve within the skill package (references/core_capabilities.md and references/workflows_and_best_practices.md are present and benign; the assets/ and templates/ paths listed as 'not found' appear to be scanner path-guessing artifacts rather than skill claims, and SKILL.md explicitly clarifies that only references/ and scripts/ are bundled). Notably, the best-practices reference actively promotes safe behavior by warning against unpickling untrusted data and recommending SMILES/SDF/RDKit binary formats instead. The only minor observation is unpinned dependency installation commands, which is informational. No malicious behavior identified.
