scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The venue-templates skill is a benign academic writing/formatting helper. Its three Python scripts perform only local, well-scoped operations: enumerating bundled LaTeX scaffolds from a hardcoded in-file dictionary, copying a bundled template to a user-specified output path with placeholder substitution, and invoking Poppler's pdfinfo/pdffonts on a user-supplied PDF via subprocess.run with a fixed argument list (no shell=True, no user-controlled command name). There are no network calls, no imports of requests/urllib/socket, no environment-variable or credential access, no eval/exec, no base64 or other obfuscation, no dependency installation, and no filesystem traversal beyond the skill's own assets directory and explicit user-provided paths. The pre-scan's flags for 'environment variable exfiltration', 'eval/exec combined with subprocess', and 'cross-file exfiltration chain' are FALSE POSITIVES: no os.environ/getenv, no eval/exec, and no outbound transmission exist anywhere in the package; the only subprocess use is a hardcoded pdfinfo/pdffonts invocation. The SKILL.md body contains no prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, or safety-bypass language; on the contrary it repeatedly instructs verification against official sources and discourages presenting scaffolds as official templates. The description accurately matches implemented behavior and is appropriately scoped (no keyword baiting or activation-priority manipulation). Bundled .tex assets and reference markdown contain only ordinary LaTeX boilerplate and writing guidance with legitimate publisher/agency URLs (nature.com, plos.org, nsf.gov, nih.gov, neurips.cc, etc.) presented as documentation for human/agent verification rather than as content to be fetched and obeyed. Only minor hygiene issues were identified: unescaped user text inserted via re.sub (regex backreference/LaTeX escaping robustness), an undeclared optional allowed-tools field, and several documented file paths that do not exist in the package.

findings.title: Unescaped user input written into LaTeX output via regex substitution
findings.description: customize_template.py inserts user-supplied --title/--authors/--affiliations/--email values into a .tex file using re.sub without escaping. Regex backreference sequences (e.g. \1, \g<0>) or LaTeX control sequences in user input can corrupt output or, if the resulting .tex is later compiled with shell-escape enabled, could contribute to command execution. Impact is limited: the script writes only to a user-specified output path and performs no compilation itself. SKILL.md already warns 'User-provided text may need LaTeX escaping.'
findings.snippet: content = re.sub(pattern, replacement, content, count=1)
findings.remediation: Use re.sub with a lambda replacement (or re.escape on replacement backslashes) to avoid backreference interpretation, and sanitize LaTeX special characters (\, {, }, $, %, &, #, _, ~, ^) in user-provided values.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The visible content of what-if-oracle is benign: SKILL.md and references/scenario-templates.md contain only a structured scenario-planning prompt framework with no prompt injection, no concealment directives, no role redefinition, no safety-bypass language, and no external URL fetching (the only links are DOI citations and a GitHub upstream reference, which are not instructed to be retrieved and executed). The description accurately matches the documented behavior, and reading its own bundled references file is normal, expected self-contained behavior.\n\nThe significant concern is a content/inventory discrepancy: the package reportedly contains 2 Python files and 1 Bash script whose contents were not provided and which are never mentioned in SKILL.md, and static analyzers flagged environment-variable access combined with outbound network calls forming a cross-file exfiltration chain across those files. Because the actual code was not supplied for review, this is rated MEDIUM (unverified but plausible credential exfiltration) rather than CRITICAL; manual inspection of the hidden scripts is required before trusting this package. Secondary issues are the missing allowed-tools/compatibility declarations and two dangling references to non-existent template files.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This is the vendored Anthropic 'xlsx' skill (openpyxl/pandas/LibreOffice workflow for Excel authoring, recalculation, and OOXML validation). No prompt injection, instruction-override, concealment directives, or capability-inflation language appears in SKILL.md; the description is narrowly scoped and matches the shipped code. The scripts contain no network egress, no credential or environment harvesting (get_soffice_env deliberately uses an allowlist so caller secrets are NOT forwarded to subprocesses), no hardcoded secrets, no base64/obfuscated payloads, and no eval/exec of dynamic strings. Subprocess calls (soffice, gcc, git, timeout) all use argument lists rather than shells, zip extraction is guarded against traversal/symlinks, and untrusted XML is parsed with defusedxml in the redlining/validate paths. The only meaningful security surface is the intentional AF_UNIX shim in scripts/office/soffice.py, which compiles a static C source with gcc at runtime and LD_PRELOADs it into soffice; the code shows awareness of the prior predictable-path hijack and mitigates it with mkdtemp. The static analyzer's 'eval/exec + subprocess' hit corresponds to that gcc/LD_PRELOAD pattern and to schema.validate()/lxml usage, not to dynamic evaluation of untrusted input. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob) are consistent with in-place file rewriting and LibreOffice invocation. Assessed as benign with low residual risk.

findings.title: Runtime C compilation and LD_PRELOAD injection into LibreOffice subprocess
findings.description: scripts/office/soffice.py writes a hardcoded C source file to a temporary directory, compiles it with gcc at runtime, and injects the resulting shared object into every soffice subprocess via LD_PRELOAD. The shim hooks socket/listen/accept/close/read and can call _exit(0) in the hooked process. While the payload is static (no network fetch, no user-controlled content) and the authors explicitly mitigated the earlier fixed-path (/tmp/lo_socket_shim.so) hijack by using mkdtemp (0700, owner-only), runtime compilation plus dynamic library injection is a powerful pattern that is indistinguishable from a code-execution stager to defenders and would become dangerous if _SHIM_SOURCE were ever tampered with in the package. Note this is a legitimate sandbox workaround for AF_UNIX restrictions, not evidence of malice.
findings.snippet:
src.write_text(_SHIM_SOURCE)
subprocess.run(["gcc", "-shared", "-fPIC", "-o", str(so), str(src), "-ldl"], check=True, capture_output=True)
...
env["LD_PRELOAD"] = str(shim)
findings.remediation: Ship the shim as a pre-built, integrity-verified artifact or make the LD_PRELOAD path opt-in via an explicit flag/environment variable; verify a checksum of the compiled .so before preloading and document the behaviour prominently in SKILL.md so operators can audit it.

findings.title: StarBasic macro written into a LibreOffice profile and executed via soffice URI
findings.description: scripts/recalc.py installs a StarBasic macro (Module1.xba) into a freshly created, per-run temporary LibreOffice user profile and then invokes it with a vnd.sun.star.script: URI to recalculate and store the workbook. The macro body is a static constant limited to calculateAll/store/close, the profile directory is created with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory (unpredictable path), and subprocess is invoked with an argument list (no shell), so command-injection risk is minimal. Flagged only as informational: macro auto-execution against user-supplied documents is inherently sensitive, and .xlsm files opened by LibreOffice with a macro-enabled profile are a residual risk surface.
findings.snippet:
(macro_dir / MACRO_FILENAME).write_text(RECALCULATE_MACRO)
cmd = ["soffice", "--headless", "--norestore", f"-env:UserInstallation={profile_url}", "vnd.sun.star.script:Standard.Module1.RecalculateAndSave?language=Basic&location=application", abs_path]
findings.remediation: Consider passing macro security options (e.g., --norestore plus a profile configured with macro security set to high for document macros) so only the bundled Standard.Module1 macro can run and any macros embedded in the processed workbook cannot execute.

findings.title: Full-workbook and full-package iteration without size limits
findings.description: recalc.py loads the workbook twice (formulas and cached values) and iterates every cell of every sheet; the validators recursively glob all XML/.rels parts of an unpacked OOXML package. With a maliciously large or deeply nested user-supplied file this could consume significant CPU/memory. Mitigating factors: LibreOffice invocation is wrapped in an explicit timeout, XML parsing of untrusted documents uses defusedxml in several paths, and zip extraction uses a safe_extract guard against path traversal and symlink entries.
findings.remediation: Impose upper bounds on workbook size, sheet/cell counts, and total uncompressed archive size before processing user-provided files.

findings.title: eval/exec combined with subprocess detected
findings.description: Dangerous combination of code execution and system commands in skills/xlsx/scripts/recalc.py
findings.remediation: Remove eval/exec or use safer alternatives

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This skill is a documentation-only reference guide for the Zarr-Python 3 library. All supplied content (SKILL.md plus five bundled reference markdown files) consists of legitimate technical documentation: array creation, chunking/compression, storage backends, Dask/Xarray integration, performance patterns, and v2-to-v3 migration notes. No prompt injection, instruction-override, concealment, or role-redefinition language was detected in any language. No executable scripts were included; the referenced 'zarr.py' and all 'assets/'/'templates/' paths are absent, which is a documentation hygiene issue rather than a security threat. Notably, the credential guidance is defensive rather than exploitative — it explicitly advises using IAM roles/workload identity, never printing or logging credential values, and not inspecting broad .env files. Installation commands use pinned versions ('zarr==3.2.1', 's3fs==2026.4.0') and advise lockfiles, showing good supply-chain hygiene; no unpinned or typosquatted packages, no GitHub installs from unknown repos. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with a docs skill that shows shell install commands, and no behavior exceeds them. All external URLs point to official zarr/xarray/dask documentation and are cited as reading material only — the skill does not instruct the agent to fetch and execute remote content. The pre-scan EVAL_SUBPROCESS signal could not be corroborated against any provided file and appears to be a false positive from generic code-fence pattern matching. Overall risk: LOW; the package appears benign.
